name: Octave Mercier
languages: Louisiana French (his grandmother's, from the Seventh Ward)
Enough French French to argue with a Paris waiter
equipment: Heavy overcoat, charcoal, bought in Marseille in 1945 with poker winnings
.32 pocket pistol (Colt Pocket Hammerless), 8 rounds loaded, kept in the desk drawer at the Statesman more often than on him, and he knows exactly why
Press card: THE CRESCENT STATESMAN, NEW ORLEANS, PRESS, in his hatband
Portable typewriter (an Underwood with a sticky e)
Notebook and pencil, a stack of them, in shorthand of his own
A clipping file in a cardboard box: every story the Statesman has run on the shipyards since 1941, and a list of sixty-one names
features: Seen Worse (Ex-Service origin: advantage on saves against being frightened and against the Shaken condition; the first time each combat he is hit by a firearm, he keeps his reaction and any readied action)

Press Pass (Reporter: crime scenes to the tape and past it with a DC 10 Persuasion check, press boxes, courtrooms and hospital lobbies; a source never gets burned, and he has advantage on Persuasion to get someone to talk off the record. The GM should play the color line honestly: in 1946 a white desk sergeant may refuse a Black reporter what he would give a white one, and that refusal is the city's injustice, not a failed check)
The Morgue (Reporter: Research checks take half the time; once per long rest, one fact the Statesman or another paper has printed about a named person, business or address, no roll)

Ink by the Barrel (Reporter, 2nd level: when he threatens to print what he knows about someone with a reputation, he may use INT for Intimidation and has advantage; if the man is connected, Heat rises by 1)
Beat: Crime Desk (Reporter, 3rd level: proficient in Forensics, and he knows which cop in each precinct will talk to the papers, including the two who will talk to the colored papers)

Follow the Money (Bookkeeper background: given a ledger, a pay sheet or an invoice and an hour, he finds any falsified entry, double set of books or dummy company without a check if the evidence is in front of him)

personality.traits: I write everything down and say very little until I have it right. I am patient with old people and impatient with editors. I dress better than a reporter is paid, because in this city a Black man in a good coat is harder to wave away.
personality.ideals: The paper of record in this town is only half the record. The other half is ours to write, and if we do not print it, it did not happen.
personality.bonds: The Statesman and Mrs. Barthé, who gave me my first job and has kept the paper alive through a depression and a war. Theo Dorsainville, who was my brother Raoul's best friend and stood with me at his grave. The sixty-one names on my list.
personality.flaws: I want the story more than I want anything, and I have more than once been ready to spend a source's safety on it before I remembered who I am. I do not trust white men who say they are on our side, and I am not always wrong, and I am not always right.

appearance: A slim, upright man of thirty-three with a narrow face, a neat moustache, rimless glasses and very clean cuffs. His charcoal Marseille overcoat is the best thing he owns. He listens with his head slightly tilted and writes without looking at the page.
backstory: Octave Mercier was raised by his grandmother on North Johnson Street in the Seventh Ward, where every second house belonged to a plasterer, a cigar-maker or a cousin, and he kept the books for his uncle's burial insurance society from the age of fifteen, which taught him that the most dangerous thing in the world is a number that does not add up. He went to Xavier on scholarship, came out in 1934 into a city that would not hire a Black accountant except to count other Black men's money, and walked into the office of the Crescent Statesman with a story about a crooked insurance agent. Mrs. Celestine Barthé printed it and hired him. In 1942 he was drafted and spent the war in a Quartermaster truck company, hauling fuel across France for an Army that would not let him eat in the same mess as the men he fuelled. His younger brother Raoul, a welder, died at Ste. Claire Marine Ways in 1944 when a staging plank gave way; the yard called it his own carelessness and paid the family nothing. Since January Octave has been working a story nobody else in the city will touch: the yard's Black welders, who did first-class work for three years at helper's pay, and were laid off in January without a dime of it. He has sixty-one names, a stack of interviews and no proof. On Friday he hears that the man who filled the yard's pay envelopes has been pulled out of the Industrial Canal.
